lesson_title: A Road Trip from Wet to Dry: South Africa's Water
hook_text: Drive from Durban to the Atlantic and watch the rivers give up, one by one.
clip_script: Load the car in Durban and drive west, and the rivers will teach you South Africa's whole water story. First crossing: the Thukela, rolling off the Drakensberg full and brown — a perennial river, flowing every single day of the year. Climb onto the plateau: now the streams keep seasonal hours — full after summer storms, sand and stones by winter. Periodic rivers. Keep going into the Kalahari edge and the rivers are just names on signboards — the Molopo, the Auob — dry beds that might not see water this year or next. Episodic. You've just driven the rainfall map: over 1 000 millimetres a year where you started, under 50 near the end. And then, in the middle of near-desert — a wide, permanent, green-edged river. The Orange. It cheats: it was filled far away in the mountains of Lesotho, and it hauls that water 2 200 kilometres across the dry west to the Atlantic. Here's the number that explains everything you saw: South Africa gets about half the world's average rain, and only 9 litres in every 100 ever reach a river. That's why we built more than 500 large dams — this country had to construct its own lakes. Want to know why your taps depend on a mountain kingdom next door? That's the next lesson.
visual_style: Dashboard-view road trip montage: lush green Drakensberg rivers fading to dry pans and windpumps; a stepped rainfall graphic sliding from 1 000 mm to 50 mm; the Orange River as a green ribbon through orange desert.
mood: Road-trip curiosity with a sobering payoff.
pacing: Steady travel rhythm, one river type per beat, the Orange as the twist, the 9 per cent figure as the landing.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to master the numbers behind South Africa's water.
